a controlled laboratory

Synthetic Speech Dynamics

A world where the whole generative mechanism is known — phone sequence to transition target to articulatory dynamics to a nonlinear acoustic map to correlated noise — built so that the latent variables can be hidden and then asked for back.

The three claims under test

hypothesis 1

Temporal variation is low-dimensional

IDENTIFIABLE

R_1 = 0.99960 already at noise scale 0.1 -- one temporal component carries almost everything. The generative rank is 2, but the second mode holds only 0.030% of the energy because the two damped responses are nearly collinear curves. detected counts by noise scale: {0.03: 1, 0.1: 1, 0.3: 1, 1.0: 1}; the true count 2 is recovered at no noise scale(s). Low-dimensionality is easy to confirm; the exact dimension is not, because a near-collinear second mode becomes statistically invisible long before it becomes physically absent.

hypothesis 2

Dynamics are identifiable only up to a change of latent coordinates

PARTIALLY IDENTIFIABLE

the two latents differ by 42% and agree to 5.74e-02 once an affine map is allowed. The recoverable object is the equivalence class (Phi, F) / coordinate changes -- Hypothesis 2, measured. a change of latent basis conjugates the state matrix, and conjugation preserves the spectrum. So the poles are the right thing to report, and A_u is not -- two estimators disagreeing about A_u may be describing exactly the same dynamics.

hypothesis 3

Explicit dynamics help where statistical models struggle

NO EFFECT (negative result)

randomising the dynamics costs at most -0.006 accuracy, and removing anticipation costs 0.230. On this task the discriminative information is in WHERE the trajectory is heading, not in HOW it gets there: a random stable system still settles on the right theta, so the class templates stay separable. Across noise levels the dynamics gap is {0.3: -0.009, 1.0: 0.006}, so this is not an artefact of an easy SNR. The honest reading is that this experiment supports the *gesture* layer of the factorisation and does not, on its own, support the *time* layer -- a task that resolves the trajectory shape rather than its endpoint would be needed for that.

  1. Which rank-1 kernel family best describes the leading temporal component? PARTIALLY IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"true kernels": "a mixture of one overdamped (zeta=7/6, omega=30) and one critically damped (zeta=1, omega=25) rise", "so the correct rank-1 answer is": "none of them exactly"}
    estimate
    {"best on held-out segments": "second_order_free (rmse 3.20e-03)", "best on temporal extrapolation": "double_exponential (rmse 8.81e-03)", "best by BIC": "second_order_free"}
    error
    0.008475 extrapolation rmse relative to the extrapolated signal scale
    control
    the spline baseline, which fits anything and extrapolates nothing

    the exponential family is the one most often assumed and it is measurably wrong here: its extrapolation rmse is 2.45e-01 against 8.81e-03 for double_exponential. A single exponential cannot have zero initial slope, and every second-order response does.

  2. Can the generating modes (omega, zeta) be recovered without assuming rank 1? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"omega": [30.0, 25.0], "zeta": [1.1666666666666667, 1.0]}
    estimate
    {"omega": [29.226709736856105, 25.08808625038536], "zeta": [1.1486307875510784, 1.008521473942706]}
    error
    0.01993 max relative error over (omega, zeta)
    control
    a 3-mode fit adds a spurious mode (omega=55.2, zeta=0.93) that absorbs the acoustic nonlinearity

    residual rmse: 1 mode 4.730e-03, 2 modes 2.445e-03 (1.93x), 3 modes 2.430e-03 (1.01x). Recovery within 5% on every replicate happens at noise scales [0.003, 0.01, 0.03] (of [0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3]); median error by scale: {0.003: 0.003, 0.01: 0.004, 0.03: 0.008, 0.1: 0.041, 0.3: 0.165}, worst-case {0.003: 0.004, 0.01: 0.006, 0.03: 0.014, 0.1: 0.673, 0.3: 0.692}. The optimiser is stable across restarts, so that spread is the *problem* being weakly identified: at noise 0.1 two very different pole pairs fit equally well to 4 significant figures. No SVD component equals a physical mode either -- singular vectors are orthogonal and the true modes are not -- so this needs the variable-projection fit, not the SVD.

  1. ORACLE -- can articulation be recovered given the true acoustic map? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"latent trajectories u(t)": "known exactly"}
    estimate
    {"noise 0.01": 0.00032, "noise 0.1": 0.00321, "noise 0.3": 0.00963, "noise 1.0": 0.0321}
    error
    0.003209 relative rmse at noise 0.1
    control
    noise 0.01 gives 3.21e-04, so the residual is noise, not bias

    with Phi known, inversion is essentially exact and degrades only as fast as the noise on the transition-averaged trajectory. The temporal inverse problem is easy; everything hard in this pipeline lives in the acoustic map.

  2. ORACLE-INPUT -- can DPhi be estimated by probing the latent state? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"DPhi(u)": "analytic, verified against finite differences to 1e-9"}
    estimate
    {"best relative error": 8.960021766428902e-06, "at (noise, n_repeat)": "(0.01, 1000)"}
    error
    8.96e-06 relative Frobenius error
    control
    the saturating map, run through the identical sweep: its optimum sits at delta = 0.03, interior to the swept range

    on the quadratic map the best step is delta = 3, an edge optimum -- and it should be an edge one: central differences truncate at O(delta^2 * third derivative) and a quadratic map has no third derivative, so the estimator is unbiased at every step and error falls as sigma/(delta sqrt(n)). The bias/variance trade-off only becomes visible on the saturating map, which is why both are swept. Reading the monotone curve as a trade-off would have been a comfortable and wrong conclusion.

  3. BLIND -- can DPhi be estimated from acoustics alone? PARTIALLY IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"column space of DPhi": "2-dimensional inside R^3"}
    estimate
    {"noise 0.01": {"subspace error": 0.106, "naive Frobenius": 1.228}, "noise 0.1": {"subspace error": 0.2856, "naive Frobenius": 1.296}, "noise 0.3": {"subspace error": 0.2991, "naive Frobenius": 1.256}, "noise 1.0": {"subspace error": 0.3078, "naive Frobenius": 1.16}}
    error
    0.2856 sin of the largest principal angle at noise 0.1
    control
    the same quantity scored in Frobenius norm, which stays near 1 at every noise level

    the tangent *subspace* is recovered (sin theta = 0.286) while the matrix itself is not (Frobenius 1.30). Blind inversion of A->B has direct error 1.21, dropping to 0.019 once an affine reparameterisation of the latent is allowed. That gap IS Hypothesis 2: what is recoverable is the equivalence class, not the coordinates.

  1. Are A_u = -M^-1 K and A_v = -M^-1 C recoverable from acoustics (with Phi known)? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"A_u": [[-900.0, 0.0], [0.0, -625.0]], "A_v": [[-70.0, 0.0], [0.0, -50.0]]}
    estimate
    {"trajectory fit": {"A_u": 0.00682261141762629, "A_v": 0.007692452638272948}, "discrete state map": {"A_u": 0.05599792500562926, "A_v": 0.053796332066705546}, "acceleration regression": {"A_u": 0.10750021269694761, "A_v": 0.10762469715927515}}
    error
    0.007692 max relative error, trajectory fit at noise 0.1
    control
    noiseless limit: trajectory fit reaches 6.8e-05

    the dynamics are identifiable; the standard recipe is what fails. At noise 0.1 the acceleration regression is off by 11% and the trajectory fit by 0.7% on the same data. Each numerical derivative multiplies noise by ~1/dt and biases the regression by errors-in-variables, so a method that never differentiates is not a refinement here -- it is the difference between an answer and no answer.

  2. How much does the smoothing choice move the acceleration-regression answer? PARTIALLY IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"A_u": [[-900.0, 0.0], [0.0, -625.0]]}

    control
    the trajectory fit, which has no smoothing parameter at all

    across Savitzky-Golay settings ['21/3', '41/4', '61/4', '81/5'] the error varies by up to 15.5x. Reported numbers above use the *best* setting per noise level, which flatters the method; an honest single-shot user would have to pick blind. This is why the smoothing sweep is part of the result and not an appendix.

  3. Are the transition targets theta recovered as a by-product? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"theta": "6 transition targets, from alpha and the phone targets"}
    estimate
    {"trajectory fit": 0.0007502457627935998, "acceleration regression": 0.0023902768377251473}

    control
    the per-transition intercept is the only place theta can enter, so a single shared intercept would bias A_u -- that variant is not fitted here for exactly that reason

    theta is far better determined than A_u: it is a location parameter read off where the trajectory is heading, while A_u is a curvature parameter read off how fast it gets there.

  1. Can an acoustic-only estimator distinguish two models related by a latent change of coordinates? NON-IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"the two worlds are observationally identical by construction": "max|clean_1 - clean_2| = 1.76e-14"}
    estimate
    {"median permutation p": 0.5174129353233831, "rejection rate at 0.05": 0.2, "replicates": 5}
    error
    1.757e-14 max absolute difference of the clean acoustics
    control
    positive control (shared-alpha world): rejects on 100% of replicates, median statistic 0.285 vs null 95th pct 0.148 -- the same test separates worlds that genuinely differ

    the twin rejects on 20% of replicates and the same-world calibrator on 0%, both at the nominal 5% level. The two worlds are not merely hard to tell apart; they are the same distribution. Any estimator that reports 'the' latent coordinates is reporting its own initialisation. Note also that the transition-*blind* version of this test has no power at all against the positive control (p = 0.88): conditioning on the transition is what makes the comparison informative.

  1. Does a global-group speaker model fail systematically on groupoid data? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"dataset A": "g_{r,q} = g_r for every phone", "dataset B": "g_{r,q} varies by phone, with deviations zero-mean across phones"}
    estimate
    {"held-out error ratio G/Gpd on group data": 1.0012, "held-out error ratio G/Gpd on groupoid data": 2.5956, "excess": 2.5926}
    error
    1.593 excess ratio above the group-data baseline
    control
    the same comparison on group data gives 1.001, which is what Gpd's 3x parameter count buys on its own

    Model G loses 160% held-out accuracy on groupoid data against 0% on group data. The gap is the phone-local part of the chart, and it cannot be absorbed by a per-speaker map at any sample size, because the phone deviations are constructed to average to zero across phones.

  2. Does that conclusion survive changes in observation noise? IDENTIFIABLE

    ground truth
    {"phone deviation magnitude": 0.07604712853141546}
    estimate
    {"0.1": 2.593, "0.3": 1.319}
    error
    — n/a (ratio by noise level)
    control
    the group world is re-fitted at every noise level as its own baseline

    the excess ratio shrinks as noise grows: at high noise the residual is dominated by observation noise that neither model can explain, so the *ratio* compresses towards 1 even though the structural mismatch is unchanged. A ratio reported without its noise level is not interpretable.

    the same models on the interpolation split, where all classes were seen

    the discriminative baselines have the class in their output space but no examples of it, so they cannot place it -- this is a statement about representation, not about optimisation, and it should be read that way. The structured model *constructs* the class from its two phone targets and an alpha prior, which is the only reason it can score above chance here.

  3. Does the structured model degrade less on an unseen speaker? PARTIALLY IDENTIFIABLE

    estimate

    error
    0.4614 accuracy drop from interpolation to unseen speaker (structured)
    control
    the interpolation split for the same model

    drop for the generic model: 0.236; for the structured model: 0.461. Both are zero-shot -- no adaptation data from the new speaker is given to anyone.

  4. ABLATION -- is it the dynamics that carry the structured model? NO EFFECT (negative result)

    ground truth
    {"randomised-dynamics ablation": "A_u, A_v replaced by a random stable system, targets and alpha untouched", "no-anticipation ablation": "alpha forced to 0, dynamics untouched"}
    estimate
    {"gap vs randomised dynamics": {"N=100": -0.006, "N=1000": -0.009}, "gap vs no anticipation": {"N=100": 0.228, "N=1000": 0.23}}
    error
    -0.006 largest accuracy gap, correct dynamics minus randomised
    control
    the no-anticipation ablation, which changes the targets instead of the dynamics

    randomising the dynamics costs at most -0.006 accuracy, and removing anticipation costs 0.230. On this task the discriminative information is in WHERE the trajectory is heading, not in HOW it gets there: a random stable system still settles on the right theta, so the class templates stay separable. Across noise levels the dynamics gap is {0.3: -0.009, 1.0: 0.006}, so this is not an artefact of an easy SNR. The honest reading is that this experiment supports the *gesture* layer of the factorisation and does not, on its own, support the *time* layer -- a task that resolves the trajectory shape rather than its endpoint would be needed for that.

    the models are trained once and tested on a world whose speaker charts they never saw.
